'''''Ageratina adenophora''''' ([[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Eupatorium adenophorum'''''), [[Common name|commonly]] known as '''Crofton weed''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Asteraceae]] native to Mexico. Originally grown as an [[ornamental plant]], it has become [[Invasive plant|invasive]] into [[farmland]] and [[bushland]] worldwide. It is toxic to horses, which develop a respiratory disease known as Numinbah horse sickness after eating it.

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Curtis's botanical magazine (Tab. 8139) (9600899296).jpg|thumb|Illustration showing plant details.]]
''Ageratina adenophora'' is known by many common names, including '''eupatory''', '''sticky eupatorium''',<ref>{{Cite journal|title=STICKY EUPATORIUM|url=https://www.cal-ipc.org/docs/ip/management/wwh/pdf/19635.pdf|journal=The Plants: How to Remove Bay Area Weeds}}</ref> '''sticky snakeroot''', '''thoroughwort''', and '''Mexican devil'''.

== Description ==
''Ageratina adenophora'' is a perennial [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] shrub that may grow to {{convert|1|or|2|m|ft}} high. It has [[Opposite leaf|opposite]] trowel-shaped [[serrated]] leaves that are {{convert|6|-|10|cm|in|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|3|-|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} in width. The small compound flowers occur in late spring and summer, and are found in clusters at the end of branches. Each flowerhead is up to 0.5 cm in the diameter and creamy white. Each small flower is followed by a small brown seed with a white feathery "parachute" that can be [[Wind dispersal|dispersed by the wind]] similar to a [[Common Dandelion|dandelion]].<ref name=Wolff99/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
[[File:Kalimunte.jpg|thumb|right|''Ageratina adenophora'' ({{Langx|ne|कालीमुन्टे|translit=kalimunte}}) plant found in [[Panchkhal|Panchkhal Valley]], Nepal]]
It is native to Mexico, but it is known in many other parts of the world as an [[introduced species]] and often a [[noxious weed]]. It has caused great economic loss in agriculture in southwestern China, and is threatening the native biodiversity there. It was first inadvertently introduced to [[Yunnan]] around 1940, and its rapid spread is due in part to its [[Allelopathy|allelopathic competition]] with other plant species.<ref name=Baruah>Baruah, N. C.; Sarma, J. C.; Sarma, S.; Sharma, R. P. "Seed germination and growth inhibitory cadinenes from ''Eupatorium adenophorum'' Spreng". ''J. Chem. Ecol.'' 1994, 20, 1885–1892.</ref> It also a weed in Australia, where it was introduced to [[Sydney]] in 1904. It has spread along the coastline of [[New South Wales]] and southern [[Queensland]].<ref name=Wolff99>{{cite book |title=Winning the war of Weeds: The Essential Gardener's Guide to Weed Identification and Control |last=Wolff |first=Mark A. |year=1999 |publisher=Kangaroo Press |location=Kenthurst, NSW |isbn=0-86417-993-6|pages=17}}</ref> It is rated a ''Class 4 Noxious Weed'' under the NSW Noxious Weeds Act of 1993.

''Ageratina adenophora'' has also spread in [[Hawaii]] and the mainland United States, where it is recognised as a weed in ten states of the [[Southern United States|South]] and [[Southwestern United States|Southwest]].<ref name=NSWag>{{PLANTS |symbol=AGAD2 |taxon=Ageratina adenophora |access-date=2008-09-20 }}</ref>

Elsewhere it is an [[invasive species]] in many tropical and subtropical countries, including northeastern India, China, [[Sri Lanka]], [[Nigeria]], [[Southeast Asia]], Australia, New Zealand, the [[Pacific Islands]], the [[Canary Islands]], some islands of [[Cabo Verde]] (it has been spotted on the island of [[Brava, Cape Verde|Brava]]), Portugal (including the [[Azores]] and [[Madeira]] islands) and [[South Africa]].<ref name=NSWag/><ref name=UC>{{cite web |url=http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=2&surveynumber=182 |title=''Ageratina adenophora'' |access-date=2008-09-20 |work=University of California website |publisher=University of California |archive-date=2006-06-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060618014611/http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=2&surveynumber=182 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>Cronk, Q. C. B. & Fuller, J. L. (1995) ''Plant invaders: the threat to natural ecosystems''. Chapman & Hall, London</ref><ref>Wang, R. & Wang, Y.-Z. (2006) Invasion dynamics and potential spread of the invasive alien plant species ''Ageratina adenophora'' (Asteraceae) in China. ''Diversity and Distributions'', 12, 397-408.</ref><ref>Lalith Gunasekera, [http://www.srilankaguardian.org/2011/09/alien-plants-invasion-in-horton-plains.html “Alien plants invasion in Horton Plains”], Sri Lanka Guardian, 23.9.2011 Accessed 19.6.2016.</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Decreto-Lei n.º 92/2019, Artigo 17º: Lista Nacional de Espécies Invasoras |url=https://diariodarepublica.pt/dr/detalhe/decreto-lei/92-2019-123025739 |publisher=[[Diário da República]] |access-date=14 September 2023}}</ref>

The plant can spread vegetatively (i.e., the stems can sprout roots and grow upon contact with earth). The seed is also carried by the wind or water and readily colonises disturbed areas, such as fields and areas near human habitation. Seed may also be transported on animals and in soil.<ref name=Wolff99/>

=== Galls ===
This species is host to the following insect induced gall ''[[Procecidochares utilis]]'' an Eupatorium Gall Fly that produces a stem gall (see image below).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2021 |title=Procecidochares utilis |url=https://gallformers.org/gall/5428 |access-date=28 March 2025 |website=gallformers.org}}</ref>[[File:Procecidochares utilis.jpg|thumb|Eupatorium Gall Fly]]

==Toxicity==
Crofton weed is toxic to livestock. Ongoing consumption of crofton weed by horses leads to chronic lung disease, known as Numinbah Horse Sickness or Tallebudgera Horse Disease in northern New South Wales and Queensland. Outbreaks occurred in Hawaii in the 1920s, and subsequently in eastern Australia and Northland in New Zealand. There are reports of farms losing all their horses to the condition. It is typified by impaired ability to work or exercise and emphysema. Pathological findings include pulmonary interstitial fibrosis and alveolar epithelisation.<ref name="Oelrichs 1995">{{cite journal|vauthors=Oelrichs PB, Calanasan CA, MacLeod JK, Seawright AA, Ng JC |date=1995|title=Isolation of a compound from ''Eupatorium adenophorum'' (Spreng.) [''Ageratina adenophora'' (Spreng.)] causing hepatotoxicity in mice|journal=Natural Toxins|volume=3|issue=5|pages=350–54|pmid=8581319|doi=10.1002/nt.2620030505}}</ref>

==Etymology==
''Ageratina'' is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]] meaning 'un-aging', in reference to the flowers keeping their color for a long time. This name was used by [[Dioscorides]] for a number of different plants.<ref name="gledhill">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 39</ref>
